noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: know the excretory products of the lungs, kidneys and skin (organs of excretion)

primer.text: Respiration and protein breakdown quietly generate chemicals your body cannot store. You have already seen urea appear as the liver's product; here you meet excretion proper — the definition, the reasons a build-up would damage cells, and the three organs that divide the removal work between them.

lessons.title: Why the Body Must Excrete
sourceHeadings: The Need for Excretion in Humans
lessons.opening: Every working cell leaves behind refuse: carbon dioxide and water from respiration, urea from surplus amino acids. Excretion is the removal of these metabolic wastes together with anything toxic or simply present in excess. Carbon dioxide dissolves in cell water to form an acid that slows the enzymes running metabolism; waste-laden fluids drag water out of cells by osmosis; and internal storage space is finite and needed for useful molecules, not rubbish.
keyPoints: Excretion removes metabolic waste, toxic materials and substances present in excess.
Aerobic respiration in cells yields carbon dioxide and water.
The liver converts surplus amino acids into urea.
Dissolved carbon dioxide acidifies cell water and slows enzyme activity.
Concentrated body fluids pull water out of cells by osmosis and derail their chemistry.

low.restatement: Cells make waste; excretion is the removal of that waste before it harms the body.
low.analogy: Empty a bin regularly and the room stays usable; let it overflow and everything nearby suffers.
low.examPointer: Name all three damage routes — acidity, osmotic drag and storage crowding — when asked why waste is dangerous.

medium.restatement: Excretion clears the products of metabolism; egestion clears undigested food.
medium.analogy: One is taking out the rubbish you made inside the house; the other is sending back the food you never cooked.
medium.examPointer: Do not offer faeces as an excretory product; examiners penalise that classic slip.

check.stem: Which reaction produces the carbon dioxide that the lungs excrete?

options.explanation: Respiration releases carbon dioxide and water as its wastes.
Building proteins consumes amino acids; it does not release carbon dioxide.
Deamination produces urea, the kidney's cargo, not the lungs'.
Photosynthesis is a plant process and consumes carbon dioxide.

check.stem: Which organ converts surplus amino acids into urea?

options.text: In the liver, from excess amino acids
options.explanation: The liver breaks surplus amino acids down, and the nitrogen ends as urea.

options.text: In the kidneys, from filtered blood
options.explanation: The kidneys excrete urea but never manufacture it.

options.text: In the lungs, from carbon dioxide
options.explanation: The lungs handle carbon dioxide and water vapour only.
Sweat carries traces of urea out, but its source is the liver via the blood.

check.stem: How does accumulated carbon dioxide damage cells?

options.text: It dissolves to form an acid that lowers pH and slows enzymes
options.explanation: The acidic solution shifts pH and enzymes lose their working range.

options.text: It blocks the nephron filters physically
options.explanation: Carbon dioxide does not clog filters; its harm is chemical.
Raised pressure is a separate risk-factor story, not the carbon dioxide route.
That is carbon monoxide's trick in the smoking note, not carbon dioxide's here.

check.stem: Which of these is NOT excretion?

options.text: Passing out undigested food as faeces
options.explanation: Faeces never entered cells, so their removal is egestion.

options.text: Releasing carbon dioxide at the lungs
options.explanation: That is the lungs' excretory role.
Urea is metabolic waste carried out by the kidneys.
Excess ions leaving via sweat fit the excretion definition.

check.stem: Why can concentrated body fluids be dangerous to cells?

options.text: They draw water out of cells by osmosis, so reactions falter
options.explanation: The osmotic pull strips cells of the water their chemistry needs.

options.text: They push extra water into cells until they burst
options.explanation: Water flows out of cells into concentrated fluids, not in.
Membranes are not dissolved by concentrated fluids here.

options.text: They cool the cells below enzyme range
options.explanation: The damage is osmotic, not thermal.

check.modelAnswer: Excretion is the removal from the body of metabolic waste, toxic materials and substances present in excess of requirements.

check.stem: Name the two wastes of aerobic respiration.
Explain why the build-up of urea would become harmful.
check.modelAnswer: Urea is a toxic product of the liver's breakdown of surplus amino acids; allowed to accumulate it raises the concentration of the body fluids, drags water out of cells by osmosis and would poison the chemistry that depends on steady conditions.

check.stem: A student claims breathing out removes 'faeces gases'. Correct the statement using the definition of excretion.
check.modelAnswer: Breathing out excretes carbon dioxide and water vapour, both genuine metabolic wastes from respiration; faeces are undigested food that never took part in metabolism, so their removal is egestion and belongs to the digestive system, not excretion.

lessons.title: The Organs of Excretion
lessons.opening: Three organs divide the excretory work between them. The kidneys take urea, surplus ions and water and send them out as urine; the lungs exhale carbon dioxide with some water vapour; the skin sweats out salts, water and a trace of urea. Blood arriving at the kidneys carries the urea the liver has made; the lungs push used air out with every breath; and the skin's sweat evaporates from the surface, lifting its cargo away.
keyPoints: The kidneys excrete urea, excess ions and water in urine.
The lungs excrete carbon dioxide and water vapour during exhalation.
The skin excretes excess mineral ions, water and a little urea in sweat.
Urea reaches the kidney by blood from the liver, its site of manufacture.
Matching each waste to its organ is a standard examination demand.

low.restatement: Kidneys, lungs and skin each carry a defined share of the excretory load.
low.analogy: Think of three exits from a building, each signed for a different kind of traffic.
low.examPointer: Practise pairing organ to product without mixing the lists up.

medium.restatement: Lungs take carbon dioxide and some water; kidneys take urea, ions and water; skin takes salts and water.
medium.analogy: Three bins at the kerb: one for gas, one for liquid waste, one for salty overflow.
medium.examPointer: Learn the pairings as a table; questions often ask for organ and product together.

check.stem: Which organ excretes most of the body's urea?

options.explanation: Urea leaves the body dissolved in the urine the kidneys produce.
The lungs send out carbon dioxide and water vapour.
Sweat carries only traces of urea; the main route is urinary.
The liver makes urea but hands it to the blood for the kidneys to remove.

check.stem: What leaves the body in sweat?

options.text: Water, excess mineral ions and a trace of urea
options.explanation: Sweat is a salty fluid carrying those three things.
Protein is far too large to leave this way.
Carbon dioxide leaves via the lungs, not the sweat glands.
Neither is a sweat ingredient; glucose is reabsorbed in the kidney.

check.stem: During exhalation, which excretory products leave the lungs?

options.explanation: Both are wastes of respiration and both leave with used air.
Those are inhaled components, not excretory products.
Those travel to the bladder, not the airway.
Water vapour accompanies it and also counts.

check.stem: Why does urea travel from the liver to the kidneys rather than being excreted at the liver?

options.text: The liver makes urea and releases it into blood, which the kidneys then filter
options.explanation: Excretion of urea is the kidney's job; the liver only supplies the raw waste.

options.text: The liver has no blood supply
options.explanation: The liver is one of the best-perfused organs in the body.

options.text: Urea becomes harmless in the blood
options.explanation: It stays toxic and must be removed; the kidneys do that.

options.text: The kidneys convert urea back to amino acids
options.explanation: No such conversion happens; urea simply leaves in urine.

check.stem: Which pairing of organ and cargo is correct?

options.explanation: Sweat carries surplus salts out with the water they dissolve in.
The lungs never handle urea.
Carbon dioxide's exit is the airway, not the urinary system.
The liver makes urea; sweating belongs to the skin.

check.stem: List the three excretory organs named in the specification.
check.modelAnswer: The lungs, the kidneys and the skin.

check.stem: State the excretory cargo of the skin.
check.modelAnswer: Excess mineral ions, water and small amounts of urea, lost in sweat.

check.stem: Explain why each excretory organ suits its particular cargo.
check.modelAnswer: The lungs already handle gas movement, so volatile carbon dioxide and vapour fit naturally; the kidneys filter blood, so dissolved urea and surplus ions are their cargo; the skin's surface glands produce a fluid, so salts and water can simply evaporate away.

check.stem: After a run, list every excretory route working harder and name what each is removing.
check.modelAnswer: Breathing deepens and quickens so the lungs expel extra carbon dioxide and water vapour; sweating increases so the skin sheds more water, salts and traces of urea; and the kidneys adjust urine volume, excreting urea and excess ions while conserving water.

glossary.definition: The removal of metabolic waste, toxic materials and substances in excess of requirements from the body.
The nitrogen-rich waste the liver makes from surplus amino acids; excreted by the kidneys in urine.
The passing out of undigested food, which never entered cells and is therefore not excretion.

figures.alt: Human outline with the three excretory organs labelled and their products listed.
figures.caption: The three organs of excretion and the cargo each one carries
